articles.title: It can be lonely at the top. And that’s just how China’s leader likes it
articles.summary: Last week Beijing’s deputy mayor was meeting with Walmart CEO John Furner and encouraging American companies to invest in China. Now he has vanished from public life, the latest to be swept up in an anti-corruption purge that has ensnared a galaxy of China’s talent: a former top judge, a spy chief, dozens of military generals – and even officials tasked with rooting out graft in the People’s Republic.
articles.body: Last week Beijing’s deputy mayor was meeting with Walmart CEO John Furner and encouraging American companies to invest in the Chinese capital. Now he has vanished from public life, the latest to be swept up in an anti-corruption campaign that has ensnared a galaxy of China’s talent: a former top judge, a spy chief, dozens of military generals – and even officials tasked with rooting out graft in the People’s Republic. In hushed tones across China party officials are wondering who is next, as the purge continues to reach into the highest echelons of the ruling Communist Party and has even toppled those seen as being close to leader Xi Jinping. The only person who doesn’t need to worry about their future is Xi himself. Unlike US President Donald Trump, who is currently battling to save his party’s fortunes at the midterm elections and is constitutionally barred from serving more than two terms, Xi’s rule over the aspiring superpower and world’s second-biggest economy has never looked more secure. He will take that confidence into a high-level closed-door meeting of more than 200 of the party elite in Beijing this week that is all set to further boost his authority – and his signature anti-corruption drive. Attendance at this meeting will be at a historic low – because of the anti-corruption measure. The meeting is being particularly closely watched because it is held just a year before an even more important gathering of Communist Party leadership next fall where Xi is expected to engineer for himself an unprecedented fourth term. The years-long anti-corruption campaign has ensured there are few, if any, figures or factions who could stand against him. Since Xi, 73, came to power over 14 years ago millions of rank-and-file officials have been purged. In 2022, Xi called to “turn the blade inward” to investigate those tasked to enforce discipline themselves. But he’s still not satisfied. Earlier this year he told party cadres that the corruption problem “remains grave” and warned that there were still many “two-faced people” in the party. The war against graft, he promised, would be a “never-ending struggle.” In recent months, the speed and scale of the anti-corruption drive have reached levels unseen in decades. According to official data from the party’s Central Commission of Discipline Inspection (CCDI), between 2012 and 2022, over 500 ministerial-level officials have been probed, later convicted, removed from their posts, and expelled from the party for corruption. In just the past three years, more than 410 officials have been purged. Some of those purges have reached places that were once considered untouchable. The party’s top military decision-making body, the usually seven-member Central Military Commission is now down to only two members – one of those being Xi himself. The 24-member politburo - the party’s top echelon - is down to only 21 members. No safe landing Over the past three weeks, ahead of the Beijing meeting, the CCDI has been sending out near daily updates of arrests, new probes and expulsions from the party. The news that Huang Qifan was being probed sent shockwaves through political circles. Huang was a longtime mayor of the megacity of Chongqing, known as a consummate political survivor who had served under six different secretaries of the Communist Party – and seen two of them go to jail, including a former rival of Xi. In retirement, Huang was prolific at conferences and on TV, giving his takes on the Chinese economy. Since his downfall, those who knew Huang have rushed to scrub all mention of their former well-connected friend and colleague from their social media accounts – a common practice in China. For Beijing deputy mayor Xia Linmao, the purge came suddenly. Only days before, state TV showed him at a meeting with Walmart’s Furner and a slew of other US executives, nodding and taking his notes as his boss invited the group to do more business in Beijing. Others simply vanished from public view, with news of their investigation not appearing for months, like Ma Xingrui, an aerospace engineer turned senior party official who once ran the vast western region of Xinjiang. The authorities announced an investigation into him in April – after he had not been seen in public for five months. Being officially investigated for corruption almost always spells the end of a political career in China, with guilty officials kept from the public eye even after they have served their sentences. And in recent months, authorities have shown they are willing to use capital punishment to enforce the party line, even for those who were once trusted aides of Xi. In May, two former defense ministers, Wei Fenghe and Li Shangfu were given suspended death sentences, with a two-year reprieve, after being convicted of bribery. Years of purging has left a generation of younger officials with fewer seniors left who can provide patronage, protection and career advancement, and the situation where the most powerful person in China does not have an apparent heir, in a break from his predecessors. And for some, that’s just fine. Deng Yuwen, a former deputy editor of the Study Times, the official publication of the party’s top training institute, told CNN that “now younger people all listen to Xi, isn’t this better? At this point, I don’t think Xi needs to worry about whether someone is already his trusted aides. “ “Whoever he promotes will become his loyalist,” said Deng. “And he has enough time to make someone his trusted loyalists.”

articles.title: US military kills five in eastern Pacific strike on suspected drug-trafficking vessel
articles.summary: Video shows a go-fast vessel erupt into a massive fireball as SOUTHCOM confirms five narco-terrorists were killed in the eastern Pacific strike.
articles.body: The U.S. military on Tuesday carried out a lethal strike on a vessel in the eastern Pacific that it said was involved in drug trafficking, killing five people it identified as "narco-terrorists," according to U.S. Southern Command (SOUTHCOM). "On October 27, under the direction of SOUTHCOM, Joint Task Force Western Hemisphere executed a lethal, kinetic strike on a go-fast vessel operating along established narco-trafficking routes in the Eastern Pacific," SOUTHCOM said in a statement. "Confirmed intelligence revealed the vessel's active involvement in narco-trafficking," the statement continued. SOUTHCOM said five people it described as narco-terrorists were killed during the operation. US FORCES OBLITERATE SUSPECTED 'NARCO-TERRORIST' VESSEL IN LETHAL EASTERN PACIFIC STRIKE, KILLING 3 Tuesday's strike was the latest in the Trump administration's monthslong campaign targeting suspected cartel vessels, which has now resulted in at least 240 deaths from more than 70 strikes, according to The Associated Press. Video of Tuesday's operation released by SOUTHCOM shows a vessel in the water before it erupts into a massive fireball. SOUTHCOM did not specify where the strike occurred beyond identifying the eastern Pacific and saying the vessel was operating along established drug-trafficking routes. US KILLS TWO 'NARCO-TERRORISTS' IN STRIKE 2 MONTHS SINCE LAST ANNOUNCED ANTI-'NARCO-TRAFFICKING' ATTACK Throughout its campaign targeting suspected drug-trafficking networks, the military has released videos and statements describing those aboard the targeted vessels as "narco-terrorists" or alleging links to designated terrorist organizations. However, it has generally not identified those killed or provided evidence that the vessels were carrying narcotics. The strikes have generated scrutiny from lawmakers, legal experts and human rights groups who have questioned the legal basis for using lethal military force against suspected traffickers outside a traditional battlefield. SOUTHCOM's continued operations in Latin America and the Caribbean come after Secretary of State Marco Rubio said last month that the U.S. was increasingly seeking to conduct counter-narcotics operations in cooperation with regional allies and in accordance with their laws. Rubio told reporters that while the U.S. has "the capacity to act unilaterally," it would rather work with its allies because that is "the most effective way to do it." THE UNLIKELY SOUTH AMERICAN ALLY HELPING LEAD TRUMP'S DRUG CARTEL CRACKDOWN Rubio also said the U.S. military would "still blow up ships if need be" and that decisions would be made on "a strike-by-strike or operation-by-operation" basis. In recent months, SOUTHCOM has also released several videos showing military personnel intercepting and boarding vessels it said were involved in narco-trafficking before removing their crews and sinking the boats. articles.title: US wild horse removal plans ruled unlawful in part as appeals court dismisses challenge to decade-long round-ups on public lands
articles.summary: The US Bureau of Land Management (BLM) approved four 10-year plans to round up and remove wild horses from public lands, but a federal court ruled parts
articles.body: The US Bureau of Land Management (BLM) approved four 10-year plans to round up and remove wild horses from public lands, but a federal court ruled parts of the programme unlawful. On February 20, 2026, the US Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit dismissed an appeal by Friends of Animals, leaving the agency to revise the plans. The dispute centred on whether officials could authorise repeated removals without reassessing horse populations, using current information and consulting independent experts. Friends of Animals’ account of the case describes the ruling as a limit on the agency’s authority to continue round-ups under long-term plans.US wild horse removal plans covered four public land areasAccording to the court opinion published by Justia, the BLM approved 10-year gathering plans for the Eagle Complex, Onaqui Mountain, Muddy Creek and Pine Nut Mountains areas. The plans allowed officials to conduct multiple round-ups to bring horse populations within approved management levels. The agency argued that achieving those targets in a single operation had become impractical as populations grew, making repeated removals necessary. Friends of Animals challenged the decisions in August 2018, arguing that the plans permitted an indefinite number of removals without specific findings about excess horses or adequate use of current information and independent consultation.Court ruled BLM could not continue round-ups without limitsThe US District Court for the District of Columbia found that the plans exceeded the BLM’s authority where they permitted further round-ups after the stated population targets had been reached. It also ruled that future removals could not rely on materially outdated information or consultations, and that the agency had a duty to act promptly. Under the Wild Free-Roaming Horses and Burros Act of 1971, the BLM must maintain current population inventories and consult relevant wildlife agencies and qualified experts when deciding whether removals are necessary. In its Wild Horse Victories account, Friends of Animals said the court required the agency to set reasonable limits on follow-up round-ups, including the information needed before further operations could take place.Appeals court dismissal leaves wild horse plans to be revisedThe US Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit dismissed the appeal on February 20, 2026, because the district court’s order sending the case back to the BLM was not a final decision. The appeals court did not overturn the lower court’s findings that parts of the plans were unlawful. Instead, it said the agency still had work to do, including clarifying when further removals could proceed and what information would be required. Friends of Animals noted that the BLM had not disputed the lower court’s findings concerning removals after approved population targets were reached or operations based on materially outdated information. The case therefore returned to the agency for further action rather than ending with a final appellate ruling on the underlying dispute.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Study to investigate sexual messaging between children and adults
articles.summary: About 1,500 youngsters aged 12-18 years old will take part in the university-led survey.
articles.body:
A study has been commissioned to examine sexual communication between children and adults on direct messaging platforms, and how it can lead to exploitation.

Anglia Ruskin University (ARU) has been commissioned to carry out the research project by the National Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children (NSPCC).

Researchers will conduct an anonymous online survey involving about 1,500 young people aged 12-18 across UK secondary schools.

Prof Samantha Lundrigan said the work was "vital" to try to prevent harmful behaviour.

The study will support the NSPCC's ongoing advocacy work with Ofcom and the government to help strengthen protections for children online.

It aims to explore the prevalence, nature and circumstances of sexual communication between children and adults through direct messaging platforms.

Lundrigan, who is director of ARU's International Policing and Public Protection Research Institute (IPPPRI), said such platforms "can form a critical part of the pathways that lead to exploitation".

"[They] can provide perpetrators with direct access to children and young people, creating opportunities for grooming and other harmful behaviours," she said.

"By gathering and analysing robust evidence, we hope to deepen understanding of how these harms occur and, crucially, identify what can be done to prevent them."

Rani Govender, head of online safety at the NSPCC, told the BBC the charity was proud to partner with Cambridge and Chelmsford-based ARU on the "crucial research".

"We know offenders are exploiting private messaging services to contact and groom children at scale, which can have devastating consequences for children's safety and wellbeing long into their futures," they said.

"To effectively prevent this abuse, we need to listen to young people and better understand how harm occurs in private messaging spaces.

"Their experiences are essential to shaping solutions that keep children safe online, and we look forward to learning from them in this research to drive safer standards in private messaging."

articles.title: Norwich Airport relies on £8 drop-off fees, says boss
articles.summary: Norwich Airport defends its charge, with the government expected to review drop-off fees nationwide.
articles.body:
An airport boss said a government review into drop-off charges came at a time when it was relying on revenue streams to make it "a viable local airport".

The Department for Transport is expected to review charges after analysis showed that prices at major UK airports had risen by a third on average since the summer of 2025.

In June, Norwich Airport increased its drop-off charge from £6 to £8 for stays of up to 20 minutes.

Richard Pace said drop-off income was an important part of its revenue that helped pay for airport operations, complying with regulation and long-term infrastructure.

Pace said the £8 fee allowed the airport to carry out different projects, including to resurface its runway in 2027.

"It is clear we need to have a variety of revenue streams to make sure that we continue to have a viable local airport," he said.

Talking about the drop-off fee, Pace told BBC Radio Norfolk: "There is no consideration to scrap it or reduce it at the moment, but clearly we will have to wait for the government's review."

At the nearest major London airport to Norwich, Stansted, drop-off charges there have recently jumped from £7 to £10.

The government said it hoped airports would "exercise restraint on rises, particularly where there are limited public transport alternatives".

Alice Macdonald, Labour MP for Norwich North, said the £8 fee at Norwich was "quite a substantial amount of money".

"I think this review is the right thing to do, and it's coming at a really timely moment," she said.

"There is evidence that fees are going up, and we need to look at whether that is having a detrimental impact and how it could be mitigated."

Talking about Norwich, Macdonald added: "We have to look at if all the public transport options are really adequate."

In September, Norfolk County Council said it was exploring whether it could repurpose Norwich Airport Park and Ride to help solve the issue of so-called fly-parking.

Fly-parking, where cars are left on nearby roads to avoid charges, has become an increasing problem in Hellesdon.

The airport serves flights by Ryanair, TUI and Loganair, offering direct flights to places including Amsterdam, Aberdeen, Malta and Faro.

articles.title: Jo Malone donates £100K for Milton Keynes cancer-detecting 'nose'
articles.summary: Scientists say the SniffSpace device could help the NHS identify cancer in patients earlier.
articles.body:
A charity says a £100,000 donation made by the perfume entrepreneur Jo Malone will accelerate work on a cancer-detecting electronic nose.

Medical Detection Dogs (MDD), based in Milton Keynes, has been working with the quantum physicist Dr Andreas Mershin for more than 10 years to develop the SniffSpace device, modelled on the scent-detection abilities of dogs.

The charity said it would install a SniffSpace in the coming months, allowing its dogs to sniff more samples in a secure room and generate more "robust data".

Chief executive Dr Claire Guest described the funding as "game-changing".

"This technology gives us an unprecedented opportunity to decode those scent signatures," she said.

The donation was made after the charity's patron, Queen Camilla, was shown how a prototype of the technology successfully detected prostate cancer from a urine sample.

A dog's nose is a highly sensitive chemical detector capable of identifying odours far beyond human and technological capacity.

MDD said that every disease has an odour and that these biochemical changes can be smelt by its canine companions, which have 300 million sensory receptors.

Humans have about five million receptors. If we can smell a teaspoon of sugar in a cup of tea, dogs can sniff out that sugar in a volume of water equivalent to two Olympic-sized swimming pools.

The electronic version of the dog's nose, created by Mershin at RealNose.ai, works on a similar basis, using protein odorant receptors to capture scent molecules from a urine sample to detect prostate cancer.

It then uses artificial intelligence (AI) to make recognisable patterns in the receptors' activation. MDD has been assisting in training this AI element.

Mershin said the charity's facilities and protocols were "cutting edge" and were "inspiring others around the planet".

Other e-noses are being used in food and beverage quality control , environmental monitoring and security and crime prevention.

The prototype electronic nose is currently "sniffing" 500 urine samples provided by patients from Milton Keynes Hospital.

MDD-trained dogs previously correctly identified which of them were cancerous.

The charity said once it had that dataset, researchers could compare its results with those of the dogs.

At the moment, the charity said its dogs sniffed samples, arranged in up to eight stands, for the odours associated with disease.

However, after each row has been sniffed, trainers have to manually record the data - and swap the samples around. SniffSpace will automatically rotate the samples, meaning more can be sniffed in a shorter space of time.

MDD said this would accelerate its ultimate aim of creating an electronic nose that can do what the dogs do, but at scale across the world.

Malone said: "My sense of smell has given me so much throughout my life. So I have always wanted to find a way of using that world of smell to give something back."

A team of dogs will now be prepared for their training on the equipment.

Mershin added: "RealNose.ai and MDD are focused on establishing a formal partnership aimed at creating in vitro diagnostic medical devices specifically for the NHS to look at as potential solutions to the prostate cancer screening and early diagnosis problems before also trying out the same olfactory approach for other cancers."

articles.title: 'Exciting' to see hundreds of Stonehenge artefacts go on loan
articles.summary: About 600 artefacts have been loaned to a Munich museum as part of a special new exhibition.
articles.body:
Hundreds of unique artefacts discovered at Stonehenge have been loaned to an archaeological museum in Germany as part of an "exciting" special exhibition.

The exhibition, entitled Stonehenge: Ancient Secrets, New Discoveries is now on display at the Archaeological State Collection in Munich until August next year.

Roughly 600 objects including antler picks, animal bones, hammer stones, earrings and a dagger have been lent by institutions including The Salisbury Museum and Wiltshire Museum.

Dr Heiner Schwarzberg, museum curator, said that Stonehenge was "a wonder of the world" and that it was an "honour" to host the exhibition.

"The exhibition has a lovely balance between mystery and new scientific discoveries and the visitors have come out in amazement," he added.

"It's not only an exhibition about Stonehenge itself, it's also about the people of Stonehenge.

"We've been really pleased with the response so far."

Adrian Green, director at Salisbury Museum, was present at the opening and said it had been "very exciting to see the items on display in Germany for the first time".

"Stonehenge is an international icon. To have it on display is a great way of showcasing not only the monument but the items discovered there."

The Wiltshire Museum in Devizes loaned about 40 pieces for the exhibition, including a large copper dagger.

Director David Dawson said the item had significance to both Wiltshire and Bavaria.

"The dagger was one of three burial objects found at Roundway Down, near Devizes.

"It is the largest copper dagger ever found in Britain, and the copper we know comes from the Eastern Alps, not too far from Munich."

He added loaning pieces to other institutions was vital to supporting the local economy and spreading knowledge across borders.

"It encourages visitors to come to Wiltshire, to come and see Stonehenge and to spend their money in Wiltshire."

articles.title: Park Hall Countryside Experience owners seek successors
articles.summary: Richard Powell and Martyn Hughes have spent 26 years building the award-winning attraction.
articles.body:
For more than a quarter of a century, Richard Powell and Martyn Hughes have welcomed families through the gates of Park Hall Countryside Experience.

They have watched children grow up, return as adults and then bring their own children through the doors.

Now, after 26 years, the pair have decided it is time for somebody else to take the attraction forward.

The farmers set up the attraction near Oswestry in 2000 with a simple aim: To give children a better understanding of farming and the countryside.

"At the time farming generally was going through a really tough time reputationally and we thought it would be really nice to educate children about farming and the wider countryside," Powell said.

What began as an educational project grew into an award-winning family attraction spread across 123 acres (50 hectares), home to animals including cows, sheep, pigs, alpacas, guinea pigs and rabbits.

Visitors can also explore a World War One trench system, a Victorian school, a soft play area and a cafe, while seasonal events such as Pumpkinfest and animal races have become fixtures in the calendar.

For Hughes, one of the most rewarding parts of the venture has been seeing generations of families return.

"We're seeing people who came as young visitors now bringing their own children," he said.

Over the years, the pair have built strong relationships with regular customers.

"They're still excited to see you," Hughes said.

The decision to sell did not come easily.

Powell said the pair eventually concluded "that perhaps both of us had done our time", while recent health issues had also helped him decide it was the right moment to step back.

Even so, neither man is willing to rush the process.

The attraction is on the market with a guide price of £999,999, but finding the right buyer is more important than securing a quick sale.

"We want to make sure we have the right buyer that can carry on our work over the future," Mr Powell said.

Keeping the attraction running has not always been straightforward.

Just a year after opening, the business was forced to close for several months during the foot-and-mouth outbreak.

"We hadn't been open very long and we had to close for four to five months and at that time there was no government support at all," Mr Powell said.

"It was very, very tough and we did wonder whether we'd be able to survive."

Years later, the coronavirus pandemic brought another enforced closure and another test of the attraction's resilience.

Despite those challenges, the business endured.

Powell plans to retire once a sale is completed, while Hughes will continue farming.

"I'm fortunate, I've still got a farm so I won't stop. Still got a little bit to do," he said.

As they look towards the future, both men say their priority is protecting what they have built, as well as the staff who helped make it a success.

They hope fresh owners will bring fresh ideas.

But above all, they want somebody who understands what Park Hall has meant to local families over the past 26 years.

"We've built a legacy that we hope someone will fulfil," Hughes said.

"You can always paint a different picture, can't you."

articles.title: ‘BJP wins through foul means’: Akhilesh alleges MLC poll fraud, warns of 2027 defeat
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Samajwadi Party supremo Akhilesh Yadav on Wednesday accused the Bharatiya Janata Party of electoral malpractice in the Uttar Pradesh
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Samajwadi Party supremo Akhilesh Yadav on Wednesday accused the Bharatiya Janata Party of electoral malpractice in the Uttar Pradesh Legislative Council (MLC) elections, alleging that irregularities during counting were part of a conspiracy to defeat SP candidate Sanjayan Tripathi.In a post on X, Akhilesh alleged that BJP leaders, their associates and officials had colluded to manipulate the counting process. He claimed that the alleged treatment of Tripathi had angered teachers and members of his community, and vowed that the SP would fight "injustice and harassment.""The corrupt BJP leaders, their conspiratorial associates and complicit officials have stooped to every possible low to win the MLC elections. The conspiracy to defeat Dr Sanjayan Tripathi has been exposed before everyone. The reason for defeating Dr Sanjayan Tripathi through vote-counting irregularities is not merely that he is an SP candidate; the main reason behind it is “Haata nahi bhaata” (he is not acceptable to them). In matters of politics, the BJP has sunk to the lowest depths. After such massive fraud, the public has realised that the BJP has, in fact, lost every seat," he wrote."BJP leaders win not through votes, but through foul means," former UP CM added.Targeting the BJP over its alleged treatment of teachers, the SP chief said the incident had left a deep impression on Tripathi's community and teachers across the state.“The way Sanjayan Tripathi has been harassed is being witnessed by his entire community. Neither his community nor any teacher in the state will forget Dr. Tripathi's tears,” the SP chief said, alleging that teachers had received nothing but humiliation from the BJP government.Akhilesh also linked the controversy to the 2027 Uttar Pradesh assembly elections, claiming that teachers would remember the alleged mistreatment when they vote.“Every teacher will always remember the despicable conspiracy to make teachers do the unwanted task of collecting fodder, and will fulfil their “guru resolve” by defeating the BJP in the 2027 assembly elections,” he wrote.Taking another swipe at the ruling party, Akhilesh said its alleged electoral tactics would not succeed across the state."The BJP's “400 BC” (a pun on char sau beesi, meaning fraud or deceit) will not work across all 403 seats," he further said.Reiterating his support for Tripathi, the SP chief added, "We stand with Sanjayan Tripathi and against every injustice and act of harassment inflicted upon him and his community. We stand united against the BJP and will continue to do so."SP candidates allege irregularities in MLC countingThe remarks came amid allegations of irregularities during the counting of votes for the Gorakhpur-Faizabad Division Teachers' constituency. SP candidate Sanjayan Tripathi and independent candidate Rajeev Yadav boycotted the counting process, accusing administrative officials and the election observer of favouring the BJP candidate.Speaking to news agency ANI, Tripathi alleged that the counting trend changed abruptly after the first three rounds, when independent candidate Rajeev Yadav was leading by around 450 votes.“We have boycotted the vote-counting process. Everything was proceeding smoothly for the first three rounds of counting; independent candidate Rajiv Yadav was leading by approximately 450 votes. Suddenly, the counting began to shift entirely in favour of the BJP candidate; the trend changed abruptly, making it appear as though the outcome had been predetermined. Consequently, we decided to boycott the process,” Tripathi said.He also alleged police misconduct and claimed that the authorities were determined to ensure the ruling party's candidate won.A day earlier, Akhilesh had urged Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar to take immediate cognisance of the alleged irregularities and ensure transparency in the counting process. He had accused officials of delaying the announcement of round-wise results and warned that the SP would launch a movement and file a case against the Election Commission if any foul play was detected.Similar allegations were raised by SP candidate Danish Akhtar over the results in the Bareilly-Moradabad Teachers' constituency. Akhtar alleged irregularities in the electoral rolls and voting process, claiming that 30 per cent of the names on the electoral roll were fraudulent. He also accused the Election Commission of failing to act despite receiving evidence and repeated representations.SP claims lead in Lucknow constituencyMeanwhile, in Lucknow, Ram Singh Rana, an SP agent for party candidate Kanti Singh, claimed on Wednesday that the party was maintaining its lead during counting. He alleged that BJP candidate Avnish Singh had repeatedly attempted to disrupt the process.“We have been steadily increasing our lead since yesterday, and it continues to grow. The opposition candidate from the BJP made several attempts to misuse power, but the Samajwadi youth did not bow down; they stood firm and remained unafraid--even when there were lathi-charges during the night, and chairs were smashed,” Rana said.Rana alleged that the opposition had tried to halt the counting process four or five times and that SP workers had faced harassment throughout the night."The opposition tried to halt the process four or five times, but no one gave in or felt intimidated. We have maintained our momentum and are moving toward victory. We faced harassment all night long. The opposition candidate, Avnish Singh, tried to stop the process five times, but we did not back down," Rana said.Sharing the vote figures after four rounds of counting, Rana said Kanti Singh had secured 25,382 votes, while the BJP candidate had received 17,797 votes.“As the counting for the fifth round begins, the margin is significant, and we are continuing to pull further ahead,” he added.Polling for five Graduates' constituencies and six Teachers' constituencies in Uttar Pradesh concluded on October 23, with counting held on October 27.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Zimbabwe’s platinum boom: Where is the wealth?
articles.summary: The metal is generating billions, but mining communities say basic services have failed to keep pace.
articles.body:
Mimosa, Zimbabwe – Zimbabwe’s platinum industry is generating billions of dollars, but residents in mining communities say roads, schools, water and other basic services have failed to keep pace with the wealth extracted from beneath their land.

Platinum prices hit an all-time high of $2,923 an ounce on January 26 during a broader precious metals rally and continued concerns over the platinum supply, according to the World Platinum Investment Council.

For Zimbabwe, home to the world’s second largest known deposits of platinum group metals (PGMs) after South Africa, the price surge offers an opportunity to increase revenue from a sector central to the economy. Mining accounts for about 75 percent of the country’s exports and about 14.5 percent of its gross domestic product, according to the International Trade Administration in the United States.

The mining sector generated a record $8.5bn in export earnings in 2025, up from $5.9bn the previous year, according to John Musekiwa, then-president of the Chamber of Mines of Zimbabwe. He said the increase was driven by strong output and favourable prices, particularly for gold and PGMs.

But in communities surrounding some of the country’s biggest platinum operations, residents said the wealth extracted from beneath their land has not translated into adequate roads, schools, water supplies and other basic services.

In Mhondoro-Ngezi, one of Zimbabwe’s major platinum-producing areas, that tension is visible on the ground.

A rich mineral belt, struggling communities

The Great Dyke, a geological formation stretching across central Zimbabwe, contains extensive deposits of PGMs. Zimplats operates mines, concentrators and processing facilities in the Mhondoro-Ngezi district there.

Inside the mining complex, ore is processed in modern facilities, and heavy trucks move between mines and plants. Outside, residents of Turf, Mamina, Murambwa and nearby villages said infrastructure has struggled to keep pace with the area’s growth.

Ernest Denhere, headman of Denhere village in Ward 3, said mining companies should leave a lasting legacy in the communities where they operate.

“We call upon Zimplats and other mines to build a road from Kadoma/Kwekwe to Turf, Benhura, Mamina, Murambwa and Kadhani, linking to the Harare-Masvingo highways,” Denhere said.

Ward 3 Councillor Emmah Chikwai said some children travel long distances to reach secondary school.

“Children from Jompani, Majoki, Maleti and Makwavarara walk between 15km and 25km [9 to 15.5 miles] to reach Musinambi Secondary School,” she said. “My appeal is for the mines to assist in setting up a satellite secondary school in Makwavarara.”

Schools, water and livelihoods under pressure

During a September 7 visit, Al Jazeera saw pupils at Turf Primary School learning under trees as rising enrolment strained the school’s facilities.

Nearby, women and young men searched through piles of waste for plastic they could sell. Cattle and goats moved among the rubbish.

For Sakina Lice, collecting plastic is how she supports her family.

“I have 11 children and nine grandchildren. Picking up plastics is the only way I survive. When I resell them, I can make maybe $20 a month,” she said.

“I am the breadwinner. My husband is late, so it is just hand to mouth. My wish is for the mine to empower women, so we can start projects and support our families.”

Residents also raised concerns about the Ngwazani River, about 100 metres (330ft) from the dump site, alleging that sewage from the mining area has entered the waterway and affected its use for household needs and small gardens.

Edson Mabure, whose family was relocated as mining activities expanded, said the river has become a problem for residents in his new community.

“Our village was where the mine is today, so we were relocated. From our new village, I cross the Ngwazani River, which is now flooded with sewage coming from the mine,” he said.

“Since the mine started operating, there is nothing tangible that has been done to leave a lasting legacy for the community. I don’t know whether the responsibility lies with the council or Zimplats.”

Agnes Handidikundiona, whom Al Jazeera met crossing the river with her children, said residents once relied on it for household activities and gardens.

“We are facing a serious challenge because the water is no longer clean,” she said. “Before the sewage spill, we used to use this water for domestic purposes, such as washing clothes and watering our nutritional gardens.”

She said flooding also has prevented some children from reaching school.

“Children from many villages cross here to go to school. Sometimes when the river is flooded, they cannot go to school. We need a footbridge here,” she said.

Ward 11 Councillor Nhomboka Kurebwa Javangwe said the area’s population has increased as mine workers and their families have moved in.

He said Zimplats has built classrooms and houses but demand continues to outstrip available facilities. He called for the company to build and operate a primary school.

Javangwe also said local councillors have limited direct access to the company.

“We do not have direct access to the mine to raise the concerns of our people,” he said, adding that only the council chairperson was authorised to meet with Zimplats officials.

The same concerns are being raised in other platinum-producing areas.

In Shurugwi, home to the Unki Platinum Mine, residents have called for more investment in local infrastructure.

“I call upon Unki to consider assisting with classroom blocks for schools, water and sanitation, and roads in Shurugwi town,” said Bulle Madzitire, chairman of the Shurugwi Residents Association.

In nearby Zvishavane, Kamino Simango, chairman of the Zvishavane Residents Association, said the Mimosa Platinum Mine should focus more on infrastructure benefitting the wider community.

Unki told Al Jazeera that it has invested an average of $1.5m a year in community development over the past five years, covering education, healthcare, water and sanitation, agriculture and infrastructure.

Its public relations manager, Evelyn Mawimba, said the mine has built 63 boreholes, supported 32 schools through its STEP-UP programme and contributed $2.75m towards land purchases and development of the Impali housing estate.

Unki also pays about $130,000 a year in municipal levies to the Shurugwi Town Council and contributes about $850,000 annually to the Tongogara Rural District Council, Mawimba said.

Mimosa did not respond to Al Jazeera’s questions despite several attempts to contact the company.

Al Jazeera also contacted the chairperson of the Mhondoro-Ngezi Rural District Council, Alderman Ephraim Pepukai Chengeta, about Zimplats’s contributions and development plans. He promised to respond but did not return calls or messages. The council’s chief executive officer, Itai A Mawonde, asked for the questions in writing.

Zimplats’s head of corporate affairs, Hama Saburi, also said he would respond but did not do so by publication.

For residents of Zimbabwe’s platinum belt, the demands are straightforward: better roads, schools, water and other services in communities living alongside some of the country’s most valuable mines.

“What is beneath our land speaks volumes,” Denhere said. “We need to see a lasting legacy for our communities.”

articles.title: Russia is selling Africa dependence disguised as partnership
articles.summary: As African leaders gather in Moscow, Russia is securing resources and protecting rulers at the expense of their people.
articles.body:
This week, Moscow will host the third Russia-Africa summit , bringing together African leaders as President Vladimir Putin seeks to expand Russia’s economic, military and political reach across the continent. Yet Russia’s growing influence has done far more to advance Moscow’s interests and protect allied rulers than to deliver the prosperity and security promised to ordinary Africans.

Putin is scheduled to cochair Thursday’s plenary session with Burundian President Evariste Ndayishimiye, current chair of the African Union. Alongside the summit, a two-day economic and humanitarian forum will discuss investment, industrial production, food security, energy, technology and payment systems. Organisers have placed trade and investment at the centre of the programme with a new plan for 2027-2029 expected to advance what they call “mutually beneficial cooperation”.

On August 20, Russian Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Maria Zakharova outlined plans for another substantial round of intergovernmental agreements and commercial contracts at the Moscow summit. The Sochi gathering in October 2019 produced 92 agreements, and Putin pledged to double annual trade to $40bn. Four years later, the July 2023 summit in St Petersburg yielded 161 more accords and a 2023-2026 action plan.

The economic results have not matched Moscow’s promises. As the 2023-2026 plan nears its conclusion, Russia’s own trade statistics expose the shortfall: Merchandise trade with Africa reached just $27.1bn in 2025 against Putin’s $40bn target.

The trade imbalance persisted into 2026 with Russia exporting $14bn in goods to Africa during the first eight months of the year while importing just $3.2bn.

Agricultural exports help explain Africa’s significant trade deficit with Russia. In the first half of 2026 alone, Russia shipped 10.2 million tonnes of wheat to Africa, with Egypt its largest agricultural customer. These supplies meet genuine food security needs, but exports of wheat and fertiliser benefit Russian producers more than they contribute to African industrial development.

Russia’s investment record exposes a substantial gap between agreements signed and projects completed. At the 2019 summit, fertiliser producer Uralchem and Angola’s Grupo Opaia agreed to build a $1.2bn ammonia and urea complex, scheduled to begin production in 2023, but Uralchem abandoned the venture that year .

Egypt offers clearer evidence of progress: Rosatom is building four nuclear reactors at El Dabaa , where more than 18,000 Egyptians are employed in their construction. But the project is being financed largely through a $25bn Russian loan that Egypt must repay with interest.

Even when Russian-backed projects advance, the contract terms determine who stands to benefit, who bears the financial risks and how public revenues will ultimately be shared. In the Republic of Congo, a proposed petroleum-products pipeline between Pointe-Noire and Brazzaville would give Russian interests 90 percent of the joint venture and Congo’s state oil company 10 percent with a 25-year concession and guaranteed transport tariffs .

In April, Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said design work would begin this year with operations planned for 2029. Russian officials have also described the pipeline as a means of protecting petroleum exports from Western sanctions imposed following Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

Russia’s commercial ambitions are matched by a widening military footprint. On October 8, Sweden’s Defence Research Agency identified at least 57 Russian military and security agreements involving 39 African countries, although many remain limited in practice. Others facilitate training and access to military infrastructure.

Russia initially relied on the Wagner Group, a Kremlin-linked mercenary network , before transferring many operations to the Ministry of Defence-controlled Africa Corps with Wagner remaining active in the Central African Republic. Russian personnel provide direct combat assistance, training and protection to allied governments, particularly in Mali and the Central African Republic.

Nonetheless, Mali exposes the limits of Russia’s military assistance. Wagner fighters and Malian troops captured Kidal , a strategic northern city, in November 2023, only to lose it to separatist rebels in April 2026. On October 6, Russian-backed forces regained the city after an air campaign prompted the rebels to withdraw. Moscow has helped Mali win territory, but it has failed to deliver lasting security for Malians .

According to the Armed Conflict Location and Event Data project, Malian forces and Russia’s Africa Corps carried out 49 air strikes from April to August, killing 89 civilians . Human Rights Watch reported that on July 10, Africa Corps fighters killed nine people, including four children , and burned homes in Bombori, a village in central Mali’s Mopti region.

Other abuses include beatings, electric shocks and waterboarding of noncombatants detained by Malian soldiers and Africa Corps personnel at a military base in Sevare from May to August.

For civilians caught between insurgents and forces sent to defeat them, Moscow’s military assistance has brought more violence and no dependable protection.

At the same time, Russia has proved its value to allied rulers in the region.

On August 29, Russia’s Africa Corps helped General Abdourahamane Tiani crush a mutiny in Niger . Russian troops provided ground and aerial support, and Moscow’s ambassador confirmed their role. While Tiani’s government survived, Nigeriens remain without political parties or an election timetable, and civil liberties are severely restricted. The junta also stripped five more exiled critics of their nationality on September 17.

In the Central African Republic, Moscow has helped President Faustin-Archange Touadera, in power for 10 years, tighten his grip on the country. On March 5, Touadera personally thanked Putin, acknowledging that Russian security forces had made possible December’s presidential election, which secured his third term despite an opposition boycott.

Wagner mercenaries continue to protect Touadera’s government while political opponents face repression and journalists risk arrest. Russian fighters have carried out killings, torture and attacks against civilians.

For continued protection of Touadera’s government, Moscow reportedly demanded close to 14 million euros ($15.7m) a month to deploy Africa Corps in place of Wagner while Russian-linked companies continued profiting from the Central African Republic’s gold resources.

Moscow is also helping friendly rulers shape the information their citizens receive. In July, Russia’s state broadcaster RT signed a content-sharing agreement with Tafouk TV, the new channel run by the military governments of Mali, Niger and Burkina Faso.

Broadcasting from Bamako since September, the station promotes official military successes, often overlooking insurgent attacks, while local journalists face arrests, disappearances and censorship. Moscow’s campaign to shape African public opinion extends beyond state broadcasters. An April 3 investigation by France 24 uncovered nearly 650 pro-Russian articles placed in 35 West African media outlets from June to October 2024. Leaked documents listed payments of $250 to $700 per article with some outlets unaware that Russian operatives had arranged the placements.

Russian-linked efforts to shape African politics are not confined to news media. In July, an Angolan court convicted two Russians associated with Africa Politology , a political influence network with ties to the Kremlin, of terrorism and espionage. Prosecutors accused them of exploiting protests over fuel prices to incite antigovernment unrest and attempting to sway Angola’s 2027 election. Igor Ratchin received an 11-year prison sentence and Lev Lakshtanov eight years, but both denied the charges and appealed.

Russia’s expanding presence is entrenching a deeply unequal and destabilising relationship in which Moscow gains preferential access to African mineral resources, strengthens its military foothold and protects illiberal rulers.

Meanwhile, ordinary Africans are forced to endure insecurity, political repression and unfulfilled development commitments. Far from delivering shared prosperity, the Kremlin is exploiting Africa’s wealth and political vulnerabilities to advance its own economic and geopolitical interests.

No power, regardless of history, deserves exemptions.

In Moscow, Africa must demand of Russia the same standards it expects of the United States, Europe and China: fair trade, productive investment, respect for sovereignty and accountability for civilian abuses.

articles.title: Continuous round-the-world cruise comes to an end as Iran war spikes fuel costs
articles.summary: A residential cruise ship that has been sailing around the world continuously for more than two years has evicted passengers in Cambodia after the fallout from the Iran war made fuel prices too expensive to continue its voyage.
articles.body: A residential cruise ship that has been sailing around the world continuously for more than two years has evicted passengers in Cambodia after the fallout from the Iran war made fuel prices too expensive to continue its voyage. The Florida-based operator of the luxury Villa Vie Odyssey announced Tuesday that it was suspending operations in Cambodia and working to identify temporary living arrangements for its residents, many of whom own cabins on the ship and live there permanently. “Since the conflict began in late February, we have taken significant steps to reduce fuel consumption, including slowing the itinerary and spending more time in port,” Villa Vie Residences said in a statement. “Those measures have not been enough to offset the extraordinary increase in fuel costs, and we have been unable to continue carrying the resulting operating losses.” CNN has reached out to Villa Vie Residences for comment. The Odyssey has been sailing continuously since it left Belfast, Northern Ireland more than two years ago, following months of delays. The 640-foot vessel is described as an “intimate” ship which offers “a new way to live,” reaching “parts of the world other ships can’t access.” A five-year residency aboard the Odyssey begins at $59,999, while a permanent cabin costs $119,999, according to the Villa Vie website. Owners also pay monthly fees, currently ranging from $3,299 to $9,500 depending on the suite, which cover food, drinks, Wi-Fi, medical visits, housekeeping and other costs. Passengers can also rent cabins from $3,499 per month. The ship was set to visit more than 400 destinations as it perpetually circumnavigated the globe, according to its website. But surging fuel costs caused by the Iran war and disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz have created “unsustainable financial pressure,” Villa Vie Residences said in its statement. According to the company, monthly fuel costs per cabin have risen from around $1,800 to as high as $8,000 in parts of Asia, which is a heavy importer of energy from the Middle East. “Passing the full increase on to residents is not a realistic solution,” said Villa Vie, adding it is working toward “restructuring and recapitalization” over the next two months but “no outcome is assured.” Holly Hennessy, who has been aboard the Odyssey with her cat Captain since the ship first set sail, said residents were given less than one day’s notice before they had to disembark, but the writing had been on the wall. “It’s been incredibly tough since the war,” Hennessy said, noting residents were asked to pay a fuel surcharge back in May. The Odyssey has been cutting back on cooling to conserve energy, she added, which would have made it uncomfortable to stay aboard the ship. Still, she said, the opportunity to live aboard the ship was “priceless.” “It was not sustainable as it was set up,” Hennessy said. “That doesn’t diminish the memories, the adventure, the very special moments of having been a true global citizen.” Sharon Lane, a retiree from California who purchased a cabin on the ship, told CNN in June she planned to live on the Odyssey as long as it was operational. Last year, the cruise company estimated the ship had 15 years of seafaring left. “This is a home,” said Lane, who poured her life savings into her cabin. “I’m just living on and loving the ship.”

articles.title: India evacuates over 180,000 as Cyclone Arnab hits coast
articles.summary: Trees crashed onto highways, electricity poles were uprooted and thousands took shelter against Arnab, a powerful cyclone that made landfall Wednesday on India’s east coast, authorities said.
articles.body: Trees crashed onto highways, electricity poles were uprooted and thousands took shelter against Arnab, a powerful cyclone that made landfall Wednesday on India’s east coast, authorities said. More than 180,000 people had been evacuated in the states of Andhra Pradesh and Odisha ahead of the cyclone’s arrival. No loss of life has been reported in either state, though power supplies have been disrupted and trees have been uprooted. Some schools have been closed and some train and flight services canceled. Arnab, classified by the India Meteorological Department as a very severe cyclonic storm, the third-highest category on its scale, made landfall on the Andhra Pradesh coast on Wednesday morning, with the cyclone’s center then moving fully inland, the agency said. Visuals on television showed trees fallen on highways as workers in rain gear worked to clear the road of branches and leaves. “No one knew whose house the water would rush into next, or whose home would be submerged,” said Nagi, a resident of Kakinada district in Andhra Pradesh, one of the areas in the path of the storm. “Trees have fallen, houses have been damaged, and all our belongings, including our books, have been destroyed,” said Nagi, who did not give a last name. Fishermen along the coast had been advised against venturing into the sea, and the weather department said it anticipated loss to crops, thatched houses and communication lines. Winds of about 78 to 84 mph and gusts of up to 93 mph are forecast, with a storm surge of about 3 to 5 feet above normal tide likely to inundate low-lying areas of Andhra Pradesh, it said. Operations at three Andhra Pradesh airports were suspended, India’s civil aviation ministry said. In neighboring Nepal, authorities suspended issuing trekking permits to high mountain areas for three days because of the risk of rains and blizzards, Gita Ghimire, information officer in the Department of Immigration, told Reuters. This is peak trekking season in Nepal, with around 750 hikers getting permits per day. On Tuesday, Nepal warned tourists against venturing into high-altitude areas due to fears that Arnab could trigger torrential downpours, snowstorms and avalanches in the Himalayan region from Thursday night through Saturday. Arnab formed over the Bay of Bengal, a major region for tropical cyclones that has spawned deadly storms on India’s east coast. A super cyclone that killed nearly 10,000 people when it hit Odisha in October 1999 remains one of the country’s deadliest natural disasters. India, however, has over the years developed early-warning systems and preventive measures to minimize loss of life.

articles.title: Cyclone Arnab makes landfall in India’s Andhra Pradesh
articles.summary: Authorities evacuate 180,000 people as storm causes flooding, disrupting flights and train schedules.
articles.body:
Cyclone Arnab has made landfall on India’s east coast, causing widespread damage and bringing heavy rainfall and wind speeds of up to 135kph (84mph).

Trees fell onto highways and power supplies were disrupted after Arnab crossed into Andhra Pradesh early on Wednesday morning.

At least 180,000 people were evacuated from Andhra Pradesh and Odisha states a day earlier. Flights and train services were cancelled, and some schools were forced to close.

Authorities say more than 12 million people live in the cyclone’s expected path.

No casualties have been reported so far.

One resident of Kakinada district in Andhra Pradesh, which lies in the storm’s path, said: “No one knew whose house the water would rush into next or whose home would be submerged.”

India’s Meteorological Department forecast a storm surge of up to 1.5m above the tide level, warning that it was likely to submerge low-lying areas in Andhra Pradesh.

Arnab made landfall as a “very severe cyclonic storm” – the third-highest category on its scale, before being downgraded to “severe” after moving further inland.

In neighbouring Nepal, authorities warned tourists on Tuesday not to enter high-altitude areas over fears Arnab could trigger torrential downpours, snowstorms and avalanches from Thursday through to Saturday.

Reuters news agency reported that authorities suspended issuing trekking permits for three days.

This is peak hiking season in Nepal, with about 750 hikers receiving permits daily.

Nepal is still recovering from a catastrophic glacial mountain collapse in August , which killed more than 1,400 people and left at least 5,000 missing.

Sri Lanka has also closed schools, with its Department of Meteorology warning the storm could trigger flash floods and landslides.
